કાંઠો. The coast

Forty kilometres of shore

Between Jafrabad and Chanch the shore carries limestone, cement, a container port, salt pans, an island of fishermen and the only wild lions in Asia. Every place on it has a name older than its industry.

NKovaya

This is not a market we travel to. It is where we live. A crew leader on our register can name the village at every bend of the road between Jafrabad and Victor, and usually a cousin in it.

Eight places

  1. KovayaHome. A village of about four thousand, a cement works and a jetty.
  2. Bhakodar pitsThe white pits, and a breakwater that was not there in 2017.
  3. JafrabadA creek of fishing boats, salt pans, and a works on the shore since 1982.
  4. BabarkotLimestone cliffs above the Arabian Sea.
  5. PipavavThe first private port in India, and the saint’s well it is named for.
  6. Shiyal BetAn island that got electricity in 2016, through a cable under the sea.
  7. RajulaThe market town, founded about 1759, and its stone.
  8. The seaTide, silt, salt and storm. The fourth wall of every site here.

The same ground, ten Marches

A satellite has passed over this coast every few days for years. We took one clear picture from each March since 2017 and put them in order. Press play.

On this coast an emergency is won or lost on the road. These are the distances we plan with.

Kovaya to Port Pipavav
About 6 km in a straight line. Longer by road, round the creek.
Kovaya to Jafrabad
About 10 km west
Kovaya to Rajula
About 15 km north
From this belt to Diu
About 78 km
From this belt to Bhavnagar
About 130 km

કોવાયા. Home

Kovaya

A village of about four thousand people on a low limestone shore, with one of India’s large cement works at its door and a jetty that walks three kilometres into the sea. Since 2015 it has also been our address.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page

  2. What you can see from the air
  3. The works at the door
  4. The limestone under everything
  5. What Kovaya gave us
  6. Ten years of the same view

The coast

Places

  • Babarkot

Where it is

Kovaya stands at 20.9065° north, 71.4535° east, in Rajula taluka of Amreli district, on the south coast of Saurashtra. The Arabian Sea is about a kilometre away. Rajula, the market town, is fifteen kilometres north. Port Pipavav is six kilometres to the east across a creek.

At the 2011 census the village counted 4,061 people.

What you can see from the air

  • The village. A tight cluster of roofs, grey against the fields.
  • The works. Immediately east of the village, the long roofs and stockyards of the cement works.
  • The jetty. A straight line leaving the shore and running east for about 3.4 kilometres before it bends to deep water. We measured it on the satellite picture.
  • The pits. West of the village, white terraces of limestone. They have their own page: Bhakodar pits.
  • The breakwater. On the shore to the south-east, a curve of rock around a new gas port.
  • The fields. Green after the monsoon, the colour of straw by May.

The works at the door

The cement works at Kovaya was built in the 1990s. Its first kiln line started in 1996 and its second in 1998. It has a captive jetty and its own power plant, and in 2024 to 2025 it made about 5.3 million tonnes of cement. It is known today as UltraTech’s Gujarat Cement Works.

We name it only to describe the place. No affiliation is implied. See Why no client is named.

What matters to a contractor is simpler. A works of that size never fully sleeps. There is a kiln burning at 1,450 degrees a kilometre from where our phone is answered.

The limestone under everything

The mining lease beside the village covers about 953 hectares. The published inspection report of the Indian Bureau of Mines records that it was executed on 1 March 1996 and runs to 28 February 2046, that the pits are opencast and fully mechanised, and that in 2021 to 2022 they raised about 3.16 million tonnes of stone.

The rock
Limestone, with marl beneath it
The benches
Four to eight metres high
The cutting
Surface miners in some pits. Drilling and blasting in others.
Overburden
Almost none. The stone starts just under the soil.

What Kovaya gave us

In 2015 one excavator and a crew of six started work from this village. The founder ran the machine alongside the crew.

A firm that starts beside a plant gate learns three things early.

  1. Which gate takes a low-loader, and at what hour

    Nobody can teach this from a city. You learn it by being turned back once.

  2. That a kiln does not care what time it is

    The first emergency call we finished came at midnight. See The midnight call.

  3. That the man you let down today is the neighbour you meet at the tea stall tomorrow

    In a village, a reputation is not a marketing matter. It is whether people return your greeting.

Ten years of the same view

Coming to Kovaya

By road
National Highway 51 runs along this coast through Rajula. Kovaya is south of it.
From Rajula
About 16 km
Nearest airports
Diu, about 78 km. Bhavnagar, about 130 km.
What to bring
Safety shoes. We have a helmet for you.

Come and see

The address and the number are on one page. Tell us when, and someone will meet you at the turning.

Contact

ભાકોદર. ખાણ

Bhakodar and the white pits

West of Kovaya the ground has been opened in white terraces for thirty years. From orbit the pits are the brightest thing on this coast by day. This is where the cement begins.

3 min read

NBhakodar limestone pits
On this page
  1. The name
  2. What the stone is
  3. How a pit is worked
  4. Watch it grow
  5. In three dimensions
  6. What a pit asks of a contractor
  7. The breakwater at the shore
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

The name

Bhakodar, also written Bhankodar, is a village about a mile from the shore and some eight miles east of Jafrabad. Records of the 1830s list it as a small estate paying tribute in its own right. It later came under Junagadh.

The name is on the map again today. The new gas port on its shore is called by it.

What the stone is

The white rock is miliolite limestone. It is named for the miliolids, sea creatures smaller than a grain of rice, whose shells make up much of it. Under the limestone lies marl, a soft lime-rich clay.

So the stone that becomes cement was once a beach. Shell, ground small, blown and washed into banks, and then cemented by time. You can still see the same material being made on the shore today. See The sea.

How a pit is worked

  1. Open the ground

    There is almost no overburden here. The stone starts just under the soil.

  2. Cut the bench

    The pit goes down in steps called benches, each four to eight metres high. In some pits a surface miner, a machine with a toothed drum, mills the rock off in thin layers and no explosive is used. In others the bench is drilled and blasted.

  3. Load and haul

    Excavators and loaders fill dump trucks. The trucks climb the haul road to the crusher.

  4. Crush and send

    The crusher breaks the stone to the size of a fist and sends it on to the works.

  5. Leave the floor safe

    A worked-out floor is graded and its edges are banked. Water finds the lowest ones. Those are the green ponds you can see from the air.

Watch it grow

This is the same ground photographed from orbit on one clear day each March. Nothing has been drawn on it.

In three dimensions

What a pit asks of a contractor

A quarry is hard on machines and unforgiving of carelessness. This is what we are called for.

Breaking
Heavy excavators with breakers, where blasting is not allowed or not wanted. See Rock breakers.
Haul roads
Built, graded, watered and kept. A haul road is a structure, and it fails like one. See Roads and drainage.
Hauling
Tippers for stone, loaded to their legal weight and no more. See Bulk haulage.
Water
Tankers for dust, and pumps to keep a floor workable before and after the monsoon.
Edges
Bunds and barriers along every bench where a vehicle runs.
Foundations
The crusher is the most violent machine in the works. Its foundation is ours to get right. See Equipment foundations.

More on quarry work is on Mining and quarrying.

The breakwater at the shore

On the shore south-east of the pits a port for liquefied natural gas has been built. In the picture of March 2017 there is only open water. Step through the years, and a line of rock leaves the beach, turns, and closes around a basin.

Somebody tipped that rock, one truck at a time.

જાફરાબાદ. Boats and salt

Jafrabad

A creek packed with fishing boats, Bombay duck drying on racks, salt pans behind the town and a cement works on the shore. Jafrabad was a port long before anyone here burned limestone.

3 min read

NJafrabad
On this page
  1. The creek
  2. The fish
  3. The salt
  4. The rulers from across the sea
  5. The buffalo
  6. The works on the shore
  7. What Jafrabad asks of a builder
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

The creek

Jafrabad sits on the west bank of a tidal creek, ten kilometres west of Kovaya. The creek is the harbour. At low water the boats sit on the mud, and at high water the whole fleet seems to lift at once.

The fish

The catch that made the town’s name is Bombay duck. It is not a duck. It is a soft, pale fish that is hung on bamboo racks in the sea wind until it is stiff enough to stack. Here it is called bumla.

Every year the boats stay in harbour through the monsoon. The fishing ban on the west coast runs from the first of June to the end of July, so that the fish can breed.

That calendar matters to a contractor. For two months in the year a great many strong and capable men are on shore. See The calendar of the coast.

The salt

Behind the town the flat ground has been divided into pans. Sea water is let in at the spring tides and moved from pan to pan as the sun thickens it. In the last pans the salt comes out as a white crust, and is raked into heaps along the bunds.

The season runs through the dry months and stops for the rains.

Salt is also the reason building is difficult here. The same wind that dries the pans carries chloride on to every structure for miles inland. See What salt does to concrete.

The rulers from across the sea

From 1759 Jafrabad was ruled together with Janjira, the island fort of the Sidis on the Konkan coast, more than three hundred kilometres away across the sea. A small town in Kathiawar was governed from a rock in the sea off Maharashtra, and it stayed that way until the princely states were merged after independence.

Jafrabad on old surveys: a view and plan from an eighteenth-century coastal survey, the taluka on a map of 1904, and a chart of anchorages on the Kathiawar coast.

The buffalo

The heavy, long-horned buffalo of Saurashtra takes its name from this town. The Jafarabadi is one of the largest breeds of buffalo in India.

The works on the shore

A cement works has stood on the shore just east of the creek since 1982, at Babarkot. It loads from its own jetty. See Babarkot.

We name the industries of this coast only to describe the place. No affiliation is implied.

What Jafrabad asks of a builder

Concrete that lasts in salt
Dense mixes, blended cements and deeper cover over the steel. See Civil and structural works.
Coatings
Steel painted to a marine schedule, and repainted on time. See Painting and corrosion protection.
Tide tables
Work at the water’s edge is planned by the tide, not by the clock.
Respect for the harbour
Our vehicles do not block a landing place. The fleet was here first.

બાબરકોટ. The cliffs

Babarkot

Between Jafrabad’s creek and the white pits the limestone meets the sea in a low cliff. At Babarkot you can read the whole coast in one face of rock.

2 min read

NBabarkot shore
On this page
  1. The cliff
  2. What the rock tells a builder
  3. The works
  4. The country behind the cliff
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

The cliff

At Babarkot the bed of miliolite limestone is ten to thirty metres thick, and it stands above the Arabian Sea in cliffs ten to twenty metres high. It is the same white rock that is dug in the pits a few kilometres east, shown here in section by the sea.

What the rock tells a builder

It is porous
Rain goes through it. A foundation here is designed knowing that the rock breathes water.
It is sometimes hollow
The sea and the rain dissolve it from inside. Before a heavy foundation is cast, somebody has to find out what is under it.
It varies
A hard cap can lie over a soft bed. A machine that cuts the first metre easily may stall on the second.
It is underlain by marl
Marl softens when wet. An excavation that reaches it needs its drainage planned before the monsoon.

More on the ground of this coast is on The ground beneath us.

The works

A cement works was established at Babarkot in 1982, on the shore, with a jetty of its own. It is the older of the two works on this stretch of coast.

We name it only to describe the place. No affiliation is implied.

The country behind the cliff

This part of Saurashtra is called Babariyawad, the country of the Babaria. Rajula is its town. The name on the cliff and the name of the country come from the same people.

પીપાવાવ. The port

Pipavav

India’s first private port stands on a creek six kilometres east of Kovaya. Containers, cars, bulk and liquids pass through it, and trains leave it two containers high. The village it is named for is older than all of it.

3 min read

NPort Pipavav
On this page
  1. The saint’s well
  2. The port in figures
  3. The railway
  4. The shipyard
  5. In three dimensions
  6. The lions at the gate

The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula

The saint’s well

The village of Pipavav lies a little inland, sixteen kilometres from Rajula. At the 2011 census it had 1,858 people. Its name is said to join two words: Pipa, for the saint Pipaji, and vav, a well. A well dug or blessed by a holy man is the kind of thing a village is named for in a dry country.

The port borrowed the name.

The port in figures

Began
Promoted in 1992. Handling cargo since 1996.
First
The first port in India built and run by a private company
Containers
Capacity of about 1.35 million boxes a year
Dry bulk
About 4 million tonnes a year
Liquids
About 2 million tonnes a year
Cars
About 250,000 a year
By sea
152 nautical miles north-west of Mumbai

Expansion has been announced: more container capacity, more room for cars, a jetty for the largest gas carriers. A port that is growing is a building site that never closes.

We name the port and its operators only to describe the place. No affiliation is implied.

The railway

A port is only as good as the line behind it. Pipavav’s runs about 270 kilometres to Surendranagar. It was the first railway in India built as a partnership between the railways and a private company, and it has carried freight since 2003.

March 2006
The first train in India to carry containers stacked two high left from here.
2021
The port was the first to be connected to the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor.
By road
An eleven-kilometre four-lane link joins the port to the highway.

The shipyard

Beside the port is a shipyard with a dry dock 662 metres long and 65 metres wide, the largest in India, served by a gantry crane that lifts 600 tonnes.

At Pipavav: a jack-up rig, and blocks of cut limestone stacked near the port.

In three dimensions

The lions at the gate

Asiatic lions have walked out of the Gir forest and reclaimed this shore. They have been seen inside the port, between stacked containers. Trains on the Pipavav line are stopped for them.

Our rules for driving here after dark are on Lion country.

What a port asks of us

Cargo that must move tonight
Tippers, trailers and bulk carriers that know the gate procedure. See Port cargo.
Heavy and awkward loads
Low-loaders, route surveys and escorts. See Heavy and oversize moves.
Yards and roads
Hardstands that carry stacked boxes and reach-stackers. See Roads and drainage.
Steel
Sheds, galleries and conveyor structures. See Structural steel erection.
People
Shift buses that arrive before the shift does. See Staff and shift transport.

More is on Ports and logistics and Shipbuilding.

શિયાળ બેટ. The island

Shiyal Bet

A kilometre and a half off the busiest quay on this coast lies an island of fishing families. For twenty years it watched the port’s lamps from the dark. Then a cable was laid under the sea.

2 min read

NShiyal Bet
On this page
  1. The island
  2. The night the light came
  3. What the island teaches a contractor
  4. The saint on the next rock
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

The island

Bet is the Gujarati word for an island, and shiyal is a jackal. The island lies in the mouth of the creek, about a kilometre and a half from Port Pipavav. Some six thousand people live on it, and nine families in ten live by fishing.

There is no bridge. Everything that reaches Shiyal Bet comes by boat: cement, vegetables, schoolteachers, brides.

The island village from the water in 2006. The port’s cranes seen from the dargah of Savai Pir. A low rock islet nearby.

The night the light came

The port began handling cargo in 1996. For twenty years its lamps burned within sight of an island that had no mains electricity.

On 11 June 2016 that ended. The state’s power company laid about six kilometres of cable under the sea from Chanch, at a cost of about 18.5 crore rupees, and switched the island on.

We had no part in that work. We tell the story because it is the truest thing we know about this coast. Industry arrives quickly here. The things that make a village’s life easier arrive more slowly, and somebody has to carry them across the water.

What the island teaches a contractor

Everything has a landing
A load is not delivered until it is off the boat and above the tide line.
The tide is the timetable
You work when the water lets you.
Neighbours can see you
An island watches the port all day. How a firm behaves on the quay is known on the island by evening.

Our own duties to the people we work beside are on Community.

The saint on the next rock

On a smaller islet nearby stands the dargah of Savai Pir, and near it a light for ships. From its steps you can see the cranes of the port.

રાજુલા. The market town

Rajula

Fifteen kilometres inland from Kovaya is the town where this coast buys its vegetables, repairs its trucks, banks its wages and finds its tradesmen. Rajula was founded about 1759. Its stone is older.

2 min read

NRajula
On this page
  1. The town
  2. The stone
  3. The country
  4. Where our people come from
  5. The college
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

The town

Rajula was founded about 1759 on the Dhatarvadi river. It is the headquarters of the taluka that contains Kovaya and Pipavav, and the chief town of the country called Babariyawad.

National Highway 51 passes through it on its way along the coast from Bhavnagar by Mahuva to Una, Somnath and Dwarka.

The stone

Long before cement, this district sold stone. Rajula stone is a limestone that can be sawn into blocks, and it has long been sent along the coast for building.

The country

Amreli district, inland from the coast: bullocks, elders, fields and a village lane.

Amreli is a farming district. Groundnut and cotton are the crops, and the rain is about twenty-five inches in a fair year. In May the ordinary afternoon is forty-one degrees.

A district like this breeds a particular kind of worker. He can fix an engine with what is in the cart. He knows what a deadline is, because a harvest is one.

Where our people come from

Most of the tradesmen on our call-up register live within an hour of Rajula. That is deliberate.

They go home
A man who sleeps in his own house is fit for work in the morning.
They are known
A fitter’s reputation in his own taluka is worth more than a certificate.
They arrive
In an emergency, the crew is twenty minutes away and not five hours.

See Careers and Proximity.

The college

There is a polytechnic in the town. Its students are welcome to ask us for site visits and first jobs. See First jobs.

દરિયો. Tide, silt, salt and storm

The sea

Every site on this coast has four walls, and the fourth one moves. The sea decides what concrete must be made of, when a jetty can be worked, and what is left standing after a bad night in May.

3 min read

NSavai Bet light
On this page
  1. Brown water
  2. Sand, grain by grain
  3. Salt in the air
  4. The calendar of the water
  5. The night of 17 May 2021
  6. The light
The coast
  • The coast overview

Places

  • Kovaya
  • Bhakodar pits
  • Jafrabad
  • Babarkot
  • Pipavav
  • Shiyal Bet
  • Rajula
  • The sea

Brown water

Look at the satellite picture and the first thing you notice is that the sea is brown. That is silt. This shore faces the mouth of the Gulf of Khambhat, whose tides are the highest in India. Near Bhavnagar the sea rises and falls by ten metres and more, and the water never stops moving long enough to drop what it carries.

The Gulf of Khambhat from orbit. The colour is sediment.

Sand, grain by grain

Pick up a handful of beach here and look closely. Much of it is not rock at all. It is shell, broken small.

This is how the limestone in the pits began. Shell sand was washed and blown into banks, and then cemented by time into the white rock that is now dug, burned and shipped. See Bhakodar pits.

Why we do not build with it

Sea sand carries salt. Used unwashed in concrete, it brings chloride to the steel from the first day. The sand in our concrete comes from approved sources and is tested. See Materials and supply.

Salt in the air

You do not need to touch the sea for it to reach you. The wind carries it. Chloride settles on reinforcement, on hydraulic rams, on bolts and on paint for miles inland.

Concrete
Dense mixes with blended cement, and more cover over the steel
Steel
Painted to a marine schedule, and inspected on a calendar
Machines
Washed down, greased, and never parked facing the wind if there is a choice

The long version is What salt does to concrete.

The calendar of the water

October to May
Fair weather. The building season.
1 June to 31 July
The fishing ban on the west coast. The boats stay in.
June to September
The monsoon. Pours, earthworks and haul roads are planned around it.
May and June, October and November
The months when cyclones form in the Arabian Sea.

See The calendar of the coast.

The night of 17 May 2021

Cyclone Tauktae came ashore on this coast, between Diu and Una, on the night of 17 May 2021. It was one of the strongest storms to strike Gujarat in living memory. The port at Pipavav was shut for about two weeks.

What that night taught the people who build here is written down in After the storm.

The light

Ships find this coast by its lights. One stands on the islet of Savai Bet, off Pipavav.
